stimulus.text:
Unemployment rate in the United States, 1940-1945 (percent of the civilian labor force). The table shows the share of the civilian labor force without work in each year.

| 1940 | 14.6% |
| 1941 | 9.9% |
| 1942 | 4.7% |
| 1943 | 1.9% |
| 1944 | 1.2% |
| 1945 | 1.9% |
stimulus.source_note: Annual averages from Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 (U.S. Census Bureau).

source: original; stimulus table from Historical Statistics of the United States
stem: A historian would most likely use this table together with the growth of war production to argue which of the following?

options.text: Massive government spending can revive a sluggish economy

options.misconception: Spending rose sharply as unemployment fell.

options.text: The Depression ended because factories closed
options.misconception: Factories expanded and hired; they did not close.

options.text: Unemployment fell because workers left the labor force
options.misconception: Millions entered the workforce, including about six million women.

rationales.A: Background from the books: massive government spending and the deficits that came with it can stimulate a sluggish economy.
rationales.B: Government spending soared in the war years while unemployment fell, the opposite of a spending cut.
rationales.C: War production meant more factories running, not factories closing.
rationales.D: The labor force grew in the war, with women and migrants joining it, not leaving it for good.
rationales.general:
1. The table shows unemployment falling from 14.6 percent to 1.2 percent in four years.
2. Background from the books: that fall came as the government spent massively on war production.
3. Factories hired millions, and the military took millions more.
4. The two trends together make the case that heavy government spending revived the economy.
Remember: two trends that move together can support a causal claim, so check what else moved with them.
